title: The One After Vegas

jokes.text: Hello, Mrs. Ross. / Well, hello, Mr. Rachel.
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel have just gotten married in Vegas; Ross greets Rachel as 'Mrs. Ross' in a traditional way.
jokes.punchline: Rachel immediately flips it and calls him 'Mr. Rachel,' asserting her identity and undercutting the traditional greeting.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — the entire joke is four words. The character integration is excellent: Rachel's independence and refusal to subordinate her identity is a core character trait, so this lands as both funny and revealing. The parallel structure of the greeting/counter-greeting is clean and satisfying.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So, Mrs. Geller!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Actually, I prefer Ms. Geller.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh, well then Mr. Green?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No, I'm taking your name.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So you're Mrs. Geller?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yes, but you can call me Rachel.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What should I call myself then? Mr. Rachel?

jokes.text: Oh, my God! Is everybody getting married?
jokes.setup: Phoebe and Joey rush into the chapel after learning Ross and Rachel got married, still in a frenzy.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's panicked, over-the-top reaction frames the Vegas wedding chaos as if marriage is contagious.
jokes.explanation: Functional reaction comedy. Phoebe's bewildered alarm is in character, and the line captures the comedic overwhelm of the moment, but it's not particularly crafted — it's a straightforward exclamation.

jokes.text: No running in the chapel. / Hey, don't you give me any of your.. Hey!
jokes.setup: An authority figure tells Phoebe not to run in the chapel.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe starts to snap back defiantly at the official and then immediately stops herself — presumably because she is in a chapel and can't finish the insult.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Phoebe's interrupted belligerence — she almost breaks the decorum of a chapel before catching herself. It's a quick visual/behavioral beat that plays well on Phoebe's impulsive personality.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We have to go to Vegas and get them annulled!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, wait. They got married by an Elvis impersonator?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, so?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So it's not legal! You have to be married by an actual minister or a justice of the peace or Cher.

jokes.text: Isn't that why you guys are here? / Yes. Why else would we be here?
jokes.setup: Joey asks if everyone is there because of Ross and Rachel's wedding message; Chandler and Monica confirm that's why they're there.
jokes.punchline: The deflection 'Why else would we be here?' implies Chandler and Monica were NOT about to get married — which of course they almost were — delivered with straight-faced cover.
jokes.explanation: Earns its rewatch bonus because the audience knows Chandler and Monica almost got married, making the defensive 'Why else would we be here?' funnier in retrospect. Good situational irony layered into a simple line.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God. What happened last night?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I have no idea. I can't remember anything after the power went out.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler... why are you in my bed?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What? I'm not— Oh God.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh God is right. We didn't...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I don't think so? I mean, I would remember that... probably...

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, we're both fully clothed, so—

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh thank God. So nothing happened.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Nothing happened? Chandler, you're my brother!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I know! Why do you think I'm so relieved?

jokes.text: Maybe you wouldn't have if you could run in the chapel!
jokes.setup: The group laments that they missed Ross and Rachel's ceremony.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe blames the chapel's no-running rule for them missing it, calling back to the earlier admonishment.
jokes.explanation: Quick callback that lands because of its logic — Phoebe actually has a point in her absurd way. The structure is clean: complaint about missing the event → blame placed on the most recent obstacle. Phoebe's indignation at decorum is a consistent character note.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, so you're telling me you two didn't... last night?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We tried, but every time things got serious, she started laughing.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, what were you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I was... being romantic.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And she laughed?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: The point is, it's hard to be intimate when someone's laughing at you.

jokes.text: I don't think they're as much dating as they are...two bottles of vodka walking around in human form.
jokes.setup: Joey says he didn't even know Ross and Rachel were dating.
jokes.punchline: Chandler corrects him with a vivid, absurd description of their actual state: they're not a couple so much as personified alcohol.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The image of 'two bottles of vodka walking around in human form' is vivid, original, and perfectly economical. It characterizes the situation with comic precision, and it sounds exactly like Chandler — sardonic, specific, and slightly literary. Well above the 8.0 anchor benchmark in originality and economy. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm too depressed to eat.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Unless... is that pizza?

jokes.text: If you marry in Vegas, you're only married in Vegas.
jokes.setup: The group reacts to Ross and Rachel's marriage, calling it insane.
jokes.punchline: Joey confidently and incorrectly states that a Vegas marriage only counts in Vegas — delivered with complete conviction, like a rule he fully believes.
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey false wisdom. The joke works because it mimics the actual Vegas slogan ('What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas') and extends it to legal matters with zero self-awareness. His follow-up 'If you marry here, you're married everywhere' and the stunned reactions ('Really? / Yeah.') make it even better. High character integration — only Joey believes and delivers this with such certainty.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: We should totally renew our friendship vows!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Phoebe, we're not married.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I know, but we should 'friendivorce' and then 'friendmarry' again!

jokes.text: Why are we in bed together? / I don't know. / Did we? / I don't know.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica wake up in bed together in Vegas, clearly having forgotten the night.
jokes.punchline: The mutual 'I don't know' to both 'why are we in bed' and 'did we...' establishes the comedic uncertainty without committing to either answer.
jokes.explanation: Functional 'morning after' sitcom comedy. The awkward mutual uncertainty is relatable and sets up the scene, but the joke itself is familiar territory for the genre. The pauses between the questions are where the comedy lives.

dialogue.line: Someone waiting for a waitress while starving

jokes.text: Do you have any clothes on? / Yes. / Really? / No.
jokes.setup: Monica asks Chandler if he has clothes on; he says yes.
jokes.punchline: When she expresses surprise, he immediately corrects himself: no, he doesn't.
jokes.explanation: Very economical four-beat exchange. The structure is tight: lie → prompt → retraction. It's a clean misdirection that gets a good laugh through its brevity and Chandler's instinctive dishonesty. Not original, but structurally near-perfect for what it is.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, Chandler was almost married? Why didn't anyone tell me?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I could've been best man! I'm way better at that than him.

jokes.text: I remember laughing. I laughed a lot. / Then we didn't have sex.
jokes.setup: Chandler shares his only memory of the night — that he laughed a lot — trying to piece together what happened.
jokes.punchline: Monica immediately concludes from this single data point that they didn't have sex.
jokes.explanation: Monica's deadpan logical leap is the joke — laughter = no sex is a sharp, confident inference delivered without a beat. It's slightly self-deprecating on Chandler's part as well. Economical and character-specific: Monica's direct, no-nonsense delivery makes this land.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, I need some relationship advice. Things with Monica are getting complicated.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Dude, you're asking the wrong guy. My love life is a disaster.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I know, but maybe you can tell me what NOT to do.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, so here's what you do: tell her you're seeing other people. Women love that. Then forget her birthday. Chicks dig guys who are forgetful. And whatever you do, don't listen to anything she says.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, that's the worst advice I've ever heard.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? It's working great for me!

jokes.text: Joey, I'm so sorry. / You want my breakfast? / Too depressed to eat. / I'll probably eat in, like, five minutes.
jokes.setup: Joey's movie has been canceled; Phoebe expresses sympathy and offers her breakfast.
jokes.punchline: Joey says he's too depressed to eat — but immediately hedges with 'I'll probably eat in, like, five minutes,' revealing that even crushing disappointment can't suppress his love of food for long.
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey food joke with great character integration. The beat — genuine grief, then immediate capitulation — is perfectly timed and shows rather than tells us who Joey is. The five-minute hedge is the specific detail that makes it work rather than a generic 'I'll eat soon.'

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We were just... organizing the closet.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, and it's very organized now. Very... vertical.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We're thinking of doing the kitchen next.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: The kitchen cabinets. Which we've been wanting to reorganize... since we've known each other. Which is a while. A really long while.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And we're very excited about it.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So excited. Could we BE more excited about kitchen organization?

jokes.text: Are you asking me to have a 'frienaissance'?
jokes.setup: Phoebe suggests the road trip is a chance to 'renew their friendship.'
jokes.punchline: Joey coins the portmanteau 'frienaissance' — a friend renaissance — with surprising linguistic creativity.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely clever neologism. The humor comes from the fact that Joey, not known for verbal sophistication, spontaneously creates a perfect portmanteau. The word itself is fun to say and sounds both pompous and affectionate at once. High quotability and originality for a single word joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: A Vegas wedding is not a real wedding!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It so is!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm drunk.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We're on vacation!

jokes.text: It's a buffet, man. / Here's where I win all my money back!
jokes.setup: Ross is hungry and looking for a waitress at breakfast.
jokes.punchline: Chandler points out it's a buffet; Ross immediately pivots to seeing it as a gambling opportunity — revealing his Vegas mindset has fully taken over.
jokes.explanation: Quick joke about the Vegas gambling mentality. Functional and gets a chuckle but doesn't have much specificity to character — this joke could belong to almost anyone at the table.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I need to find a divorce lawyer.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: At this point, shouldn't your lawyer just buy you a condo?

jokes.text: And who was gonna be your best man? Don't say Ross. Do not say Ross.
jokes.setup: Joey learns Chandler and Monica almost got married without telling anyone.
jokes.punchline: Joey's first concern is not their feelings or the relationship — it's whether Ross would have been best man over him.
jokes.explanation: Good character-specific comedy. Joey's self-centered priorities — skipping past the emotional gravity of the moment to focus on his own potential slight — is very Joey. The repeated 'Do not say Ross' has escalating energy.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm going to get an annulment.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: An annulment? What's that?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's like the marriage never happened.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you can do that? I thought you just had to get a divorce!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, an annulment is different. It's like... it erases the marriage from history.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, so it's like a medical procedure? Like you go in and they just... remove it?

jokes.text: Tell her she's not marriage material. / Girls say it to me all the time.
jokes.setup: Chandler asks Joey how to tell Monica he doesn't think they're ready to get married without crushing her.
jokes.punchline: Joey advises Chandler to tell Monica she's 'not marriage material' — a phrase that women apparently use on Joey regularly, which he has somehow internalized as helpful wisdom.
jokes.explanation: Strong Joey joke. The double laugh comes from (1) the absurdity of the advice itself and (2) the revelation that women tell this to Joey constantly. Joey's complete lack of self-awareness in offering this as wisdom — and his confidence that Monica will be 'relieved' — is pitch-perfect character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You married divorce?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, I didn't marry divorce.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You're literally married to divorce. You have divorce's last name.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That's not... I have my own last name.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You have three of your own last names because you keep marrying and divorcing.

jokes.text: We were just talking about bacon. / No, we were talking about tennis. / Tennis is more believable.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica are caught mid-conversation about whether to get married; they scramble for a cover story.
jokes.punchline: Chandler says bacon; Monica corrects to tennis; then Chandler agrees tennis is more believable as a cover — the meta-commentary on their own lying is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Very well-constructed three-beat exchange. The escalation from bad lie to slightly less bad lie to self-aware acknowledgment is clean. 'Tennis is more believable' as a deadpan verdict from Chandler lands well. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I'm just... I'm really bad at this. I can't tell jokes. I always mess them up.

jokes.text: Ross invited us all to watch.
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel insist nothing happened last night; Phoebe then drops context that completely reframes the conversation.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe casually mentions Ross invited them to watch — which, in context, sounds deeply wrong before clarifying she means the wedding.
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection. The line is deliberately ambiguous — 'Ross invited us all to watch' — landing in the middle of a conversation about whether Ross and Rachel did anything inappropriate. The pause before the reveal (marked by [07:23]) is what sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I got it. Heads we get married, tails we don't.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler, that's a coin.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I know, but I shaved one side.

jokes.text: You did. / What? / Hello. We didn't get married. / No, we didn't. That's ridi..
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel are told they got married; they react with disbelief.
jokes.punchline: Their confident denials trail off as the realization visually dawns — the audience knows before they do.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the dawning horror on their faces as denial collapses. Standard sitcom revelation structure but effectively executed. The cut-off 'That's ridi—' works as a visual beat.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: An eight? Marriage! Oh no!

jokes.text: They let you get married. / Most people who marry in Vegas are drunk. / Now, I'm drunk right now.
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel claim the chapel wouldn't have let them marry if they were that drunk.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe corrects them — drunkenness is the norm in Vegas — and Chandler casually admits he's drunk right now, at breakfast.
jokes.explanation: Two good jokes stacked: Phoebe's accurate-but-blunt correction of Vegas norms, then Chandler's breezy confession of current drunkenness as a non-sequitur. The 'Now, I'm drunk right now' beat is funny because of its casual matter-of-factness.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey fell asleep before we even got out of the parking lot.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: That's because he's a baby.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I am not a baby! I was just resting my eyes.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, you were snoring before we hit the highway.

jokes.text: I can't have a mimosa with breakfast? I'm on vacation.
jokes.setup: Everyone reacts to Chandler admitting he's drunk.
jokes.punchline: Chandler defends himself with the most reasonable possible framing — a mimosa is brunch appropriate — as if that explains everything.
jokes.explanation: Chandler's self-defense logic is pitch-perfect: escalate the admission to 'drunk' and then retreat to 'mimosa at brunch' as if the two are equivalent. The 'I'm on vacation' kicker adds an extra layer of rationalization.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You're like a sleeping dragon sitting on a pile of gold, except the gold is my time and you're just hoarding it while you drool!

jokes.text: Well, I think.. I think Ross already has one. / Yeah, that guy's finally gonna be able to put in that pool.
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel discuss finding a divorce lawyer.
jokes.punchline: Chandler notes Ross already has a divorce lawyer; Joey adds that the lawyer is so wealthy from Ross's business that he can finally afford a pool.
jokes.explanation: Joey's specific detail about the pool elevates what could have been a simple joke about Ross's divorce rate. The image of a lawyer so enriched by one client that he can build a pool is vivid and funny. Good escalation on the base premise.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Are my eyes open?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh my God!

jokes.text: Now, this one's free, right? Because you paid for the first two.
jokes.setup: Ross says they don't need a divorce lawyer because they'll just get an annulment.
jokes.punchline: Chandler asks if the divorce lawyer is now free since Ross paid for two divorces already — like a frequent customer.
jokes.explanation: The 'buy two get one free' framing applied to divorces is a good joke. Economically written and delivers the laugh quickly. Good deployment of Ross's divorce history as comedic fodder.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. I'll stay married to you.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah, but we have to take this seriously. We need to act like a real married couple.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay...

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: That means no more going out with other people, no more flirting, and we have to spend every night together.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wait, wait. I thought this was supposed to be fake?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It is fake, but we have to make it look real.

jokes.text: Ross, I don't think surgery is the answer here.
jokes.setup: Ross explains they're going to get an annulment rather than a divorce.
jokes.punchline: Rachel mishears 'annulment' as something surgical, suggesting her hungover brain has completely misfired.
jokes.explanation: Classic malapropism-adjacent joke. The humor is in Rachel genuinely confusing the word with something medical — perhaps conflating it with 'nullment' or imagining some physical procedure. Good economy; works better in performance than on the page.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You have to check the box. It's important. Are you Miss or Mrs?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I don't know, I'll just check Miss.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, you should think about it. What if you get married?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Fine, fine. I'll check Mrs. Happy now?

jokes.text: Oh, that's your thing! / What? / Your thing. You're the guy who gets divorced.
jokes.setup: Ross protests that he doesn't want a divorce.
jokes.punchline: Chandler establishes that getting divorced is simply Ross's 'thing' — his defining character trait.
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy built on Ross's history. 'The guy who gets divorced' as a social identity is a clean, mean-spirited-but-affectionate label. Sets up the escalation that follows.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Rachel, I need to ask you a favor.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What is it?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Will you marry me?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What?!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, you're always doing favors for people. I figured if we were married, you'd have to do this one.

jokes.text: You love divorce so much, you're probably gonna marry it...and then it won't work out, so you're gonna have to divorce it.
jokes.setup: Chandler has established that divorce is Ross's 'thing'; Ross denies loving divorce.
jokes.punchline: Chandler extends the logic to its absurd conclusion: Ross will marry divorce and then divorce divorce.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The logic is airtight in its absurdity: take the premise (Ross loves divorce) and follow it to its recursive conclusion (he'll divorce divorce). The structure is a perfect escalation with a satisfying twist at the end. The joke earns the laugh through comedic logic rather than shock or reference — Chandler's delivery would seal it. Approaches the 8.0 craft anchor benchmark.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What if I pick up a hitchhiker and he's a serial killer?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, you know, you just gotta play it cool. Ask him questions. Make him feel like you're interested.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What kind of questions?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I don't know, like... 'So, have you killed anyone today?'

jokes.text: I'm so drunk.
jokes.setup: Chandler has just delivered a complicated, well-structured logical riff about Ross marrying and divorcing divorce.
jokes.punchline: He immediately undercuts his own eloquence by noting he's drunk — implying the speech came from somewhere unexpected.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the 'marry divorce' speech. Three words undercut everything that just came before — and they work because the speech was actually logically coherent, making the drunken admission funnier. Maximum economy (three words, peak effect). The running gag of Chandler's vacation drunkenness pays off here.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: So where exactly are you taking me?

dialogue.speaker: Hitchhiker
dialogue.line: Just down the road a bit.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: And what are your intentions?

dialogue.speaker: Hitchhiker
dialogue.line: Well, I thought we'd stop for coffee.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh! Do you have any splenda?

jokes.text: I can't believe I rolled an eight. / That was so unlikely.
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler agreed to get married only if she rolls an eight — with eleven ways not to roll an eight versus one way to roll it. She rolls an eight.
jokes.punchline: Their shared understatement ('so unlikely') about a genuinely improbable event plays perfectly flat against the comedic stakes.
jokes.explanation: Good deadpan reaction to an improbable event. The understated 'That was so unlikely' earns the laugh through flatness when the moment calls for panic. Structurally functional but not highly original.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: We can't stay married. It's like... it's like trying to fit a square peg in a round hole.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Rachel, that's the whole point of marriage, compromise—

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No, no, no. It's like a children's book! 'The Little Square Peg Who Couldn't Find His Hole.' We could illustrate it!

jokes.text: Last night I rolled a hard eight. / It was the wrong kind of eight. No wedding! Damn it! / I wanted it so bad!
jokes.setup: Chandler reveals that he rolled a 'hard eight' the night before, referencing the earlier scene where they almost decided to get married.
jokes.punchline: Monica's devastated 'No wedding! Damn it! I wanted it so bad!' reveals how much she actually did want to marry Chandler — hilariously undercutting her earlier hesitation.
jokes.explanation: Monica's explosive 'I wanted it so bad!' is the comedic payoff of her entire arc in this scene. The irony is rich: she spent the episode worrying about how to tell Chandler she wasn't ready, and her true feelings burst out in this moment of disappointment. Good character integration and an earned reversal.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: A marriage is like a hangover — you wake up and wonder what you did last night, and there's nothing you can do about it now.

jokes.text: Okay, you have 19 questions left. Use them wisely.
jokes.setup: Phoebe and Joey are playing 20 Questions on their road trip; Joey apparently asked one question.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe gravely informs Joey he has 19 questions left, treating the game like a precious finite resource.
jokes.explanation: Light but effective. Phoebe's earnest commitment to game rules and the portentous 'use them wisely' is a good character beat. The setup implies Joey burned his first question on something trivial.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You know what? Fine. I'll get the annulment.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah. And you know what else? I'm gonna throw my ring in the river, you're gonna catch the bouquet, and we're gonna have a big reception where everyone throws rice at us as we leave!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross...

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: And the best part? We get to do the whole thing again in five years!

jokes.text: We've been on the road for 6 hours, and you've been asleep for 5 and a half.
jokes.setup: Joey promised Phoebe a fun road trip and hasn't delivered.
jokes.punchline: The specific accounting — 6 hours of travel, 5.5 hours asleep — is the comedic detail that makes the grievance feel precise and genuinely aggrieved.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of the numbers is what makes it funny. 'Most of the time' wouldn't work — 5.5 out of 6 hours gives it a documentary precision that sells Phoebe's indignation. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, so you can reach me at the coffee shop, or you can leave a message at the hostel, or you can just... yell really loud and I'll probably hear you.

jokes.text: That will be your punishment, you greedy sleeper!
jokes.setup: Phoebe tells Joey his punishment for sleeping the whole trip is that he has to drive.
jokes.punchline: 'Greedy sleeper' as an insult is an inherently absurd construction — sleep-hoarding as a character flaw.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's invented moral framework — where hogging sleep is a form of greed — is exactly her character. 'Greedy sleeper' is a genuinely fun coinage and an example of Phoebe's unique ethical indignation. Quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Ground control to Major Tom. Ground control to Major Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, you can stop now.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Take your protein pills and put your helmet on.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I said stop! Stop it!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Ground control to Major Tom, commencing countdown...

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Fine! Fine, you win! I'm not mad anymore!

jokes.text: ...because the radio's broken and you are selfish, but you have a nice voice.
jokes.setup: Phoebe demands Joey sing because the radio is broken.
jokes.punchline: The pivot from 'you are selfish' to 'but you have a nice voice' as if these are equally weighted facts is the joke — Phoebe's moral accounting is both damning and complimentary in the same breath.
jokes.explanation: Good Phoebe line. The 'but you have a nice voice' softens nothing while pretending to soften everything. The juxtaposition of condemnation and compliment in the same clause is exactly Phoebe's brand of unfiltered sincerity.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm sorry I fell asleep on the road trip.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: It's okay, you can still sleep normally.

jokes.text: Joey sings a rock anthem enthusiastically in the cab.
jokes.setup: Phoebe commands Joey to sing since the radio is broken.
jokes.punchline: Joey launches into an enthusiastic rock performance in the cab — the visual of Joey belting rock in a moving taxi is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The visual/physical comedy of Joey's earnest rock performance in a cab is functional. It plays better on screen than on paper. Joey's commitment to whatever he's doing — including this — is always character-appropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay Joey, I'm thinking of something.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Is it food?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: We're done here.

jokes.text: Are my eyes open? / No!
jokes.setup: Joey is driving the cab after being forced to switch; Phoebe checks on him.
jokes.punchline: Joey is driving with his eyes closed — he asks if they're open, they're not.
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy inferred from dialogue. The terror of Joey driving with eyes closed, combined with his drowsy confusion about his own open eyes, is a good visual gag. Maximum economy — two words and a reply.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Don't! Don't say it!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Whatever you're about to say, just don't!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I was just going to say we should get out of here.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh. Okay then.

jokes.text: Hey, hubby.
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel wake up the morning after getting married in Vegas.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's breezy 'hubby' greeting treats the accidental marriage with casual irony — neither panic nor romance.
jokes.explanation: One-word joke that lands through tone. 'Hubby' is exactly the right degree of breezy irony to open the morning-after scene. Very economical.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I don't want things to change.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I like things the way they are. I like my apartment, I like my job, I like my—

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, is that a stain on the couch?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, that's a stain. That's a stain! Where did that come from? How long has that been there?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I need to get some club soda. NOW.

jokes.text: Wow, this is so amazing. / I really thought I'd have to talk you into this more. / Now I'm scared because I don't actually think you're kidding.
jokes.setup: Ross floats the idea of staying married; Rachel seems to agree enthusiastically.
jokes.punchline: Ross realizes with dawning horror that Rachel is not joking and might genuinely want to stay married — the roles have reversed from what he expected.
jokes.explanation: Good reversal. Ross, who actually wants to stay married, is terrified when Rachel agrees too convincingly — suggesting she may have her own reasons. The escalating dread in 'Now I'm scared because I don't actually think you're kidding' is a nice subversion.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I wanted to give you a key to the apartment.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: A key? That's so romantic!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, you're here all the time anyway.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh. So this is less 'I love you' and more 'stop ringing the doorbell'?

jokes.text: I mean, you fill some form out once in a while...instead of checking the box 'Miss,' you check the box that says, 'Mrs.' / It's right next to it.
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to convince Rachel that staying married won't really affect her life.
jokes.punchline: His entire pitch for why marriage is no burden is that Rachel will have to check a slightly different checkbox on forms — and he even reassures her that it's 'right next to it.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent Ross-specific character comedy. His obliviousness is on full display — reducing marriage to a paperwork inconvenience and then carefully reassuring Rachel that the checkbox is conveniently adjacent. The 'It's right next to it' kicker is what elevates this from good to great. Perfect character integration: only Ross would think this is a compelling argument.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I can't believe I'm actually doing this. The ceremonial key to the new apartment!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Here we go...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh God, oh God, it's not turning!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Just push harder!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I AM pushing! This is a sign. This is definitely a sign!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It's not a sign, the lock is just stuck.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, no, no. A ceremonial key that doesn't work? How is that not a sign?!

jokes.text: Okay. I'm sorry, you're right. You know what? We can stay married...because I thought that the boxes were far away from each other.
jokes.setup: Ross has just argued that staying married is barely an inconvenience — just a different checkbox.
jokes.punchline: Rachel sarcastically agrees to stay married, citing the checkbox proximity as her deciding factor — demolishing Ross's entire argument by playing it straight.
jokes.explanation: The perfect callback to the checkbox joke. Rachel accepting Ross's absurd logic on its own terms — 'I thought the boxes were far away from each other' — is a devastating and very funny mock-agreement. Approaches the 8.0 craft benchmark: the structure is clean, the character voice is perfect, and the economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm not hugging the door!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I'm definitely not hugging the door.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Good, because I wasn't planning to.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So we're both just standing here, not hugging this door.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Exactly. Not hugging it at all.

jokes.text: And as my wife, I think you should grant me this favor.
jokes.setup: Ross is pleading with Rachel not to get the annulment; he invokes her status as his wife.
jokes.punchline: Ross uses being married as leverage to ask Rachel to stay married — a circular, self-serving argument he delivers earnestly.
jokes.explanation: Ross's circular logic is a good character beat. Using the marriage to justify preserving the marriage is exactly the kind of self-serving reasoning Ross engages in. Not the sharpest joke but lands as a character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You guys, I can't go to the movies. I already saw a movie.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: When?

jokes.text: That kid kicked me really hard. / Well, you did pull his hair. / He took my snack.
jokes.setup: During the road trip, something has happened with a child on the route.
jokes.punchline: Joey was kicked by a child; when Phoebe points out he pulled the kid's hair, Joey defends himself — 'He took my snack' — suggesting a fully adult man got into a physical altercation with a child over food.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best visual comedy moments. Joey pulling a child's hair over a snack is perfectly in character — his food obsession escalated to a physical confrontation with a minor. The three-beat escalation (kicked → hair pull → snack theft) builds perfectly. 'He took my snack' as a full justification is very Joey and very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay, I lied. I didn't get the annulment.

jokes.text: How could you pick up a hitchhiker? He could be a rap.. He could be a rapist or a killer or something. / Don't you think I asked him that before he got in?
jokes.setup: Phoebe discovers Joey has picked up a hitchhiker.
jokes.punchline: Joey's defense: he screened the hitchhiker first by asking if he was a rapist — as if a rapist would self-identify.
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey logic. His pre-screening method — asking the hitchhiker if he's a rapist — is absurdly reasonable from Joey's perspective, completely insane from anyone else's. The question 'Don't you think I asked him that before he got in?' is delivered with genuine indignation, as if Phoebe is the unreasonable one. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wow, Joey, great job. You've really outdone yourself. The lock was broken before, but now the door's falling off its hinges. That's... that's really impressive work.

jokes.text: I'm not talking to you. You go back to sleep. / And, you, are you a rapist? / No. / Do you like car games?
jokes.setup: Phoebe is furious at Joey for the hitchhiker; she dismisses Joey and turns to the hitchhiker.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe immediately accepts the hitchhiker after his 'No' and pivots to asking if he likes car games — accepting his self-report at face value just as Joey did.
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback and escalation. Phoebe, who was horrified at Joey's naivety, immediately replicates the exact same behavior — accepts 'No' as proof of innocence and moves straight to car games. The irony lands hard and the transition to 'Do you like car games?' is perfectly abrupt. One of the best comedy beats in the episode.

jokes.text: Yeah, you know the license plate game? / I love the license plate game! / I'll play. I'll play. / No, you need your sleep. Night-night.
jokes.setup: The hitchhiker wants to join the car game; Joey tries to participate.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe shuts Joey out of his own cab's game and sends him to sleep — the hitchhiker has displaced Joey in his own vehicle.
jokes.explanation: Good payoff on the hitchhiker setup. Phoebe bonding with the stranger over the license plate game and dismissing Joey with a condescending 'Night-night' is a satisfying role reversal and character-specific to Phoebe's mercurial affections.

jokes.text: We register...and you get to keep all the presents.
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to persuade Rachel to stay married by pitching the benefits.
jokes.punchline: His strongest argument: they can register for gifts and keep them. Ross reduces marriage to its material perks.
jokes.explanation: Ross's persuasion tactics are increasingly desperate, and the pivot to 'you can keep the presents' as a marriage incentive is both funny and sad. It reveals how out of touch he is with what Rachel actually values.

jokes.text: I came up with an analogy about a little goldfish in a pond that freezes over in the winter...but I realized that was a story about what to do when people pick on you. So I'm gonna actually save that for my children's book.
jokes.setup: Rachel is trying to tell Ross they can't stay married and says she thought of an analogy.
jokes.punchline: The analogy she prepared is completely wrong for the situation — it's about handling bullying — and she pivots to saving it for a children's book she apparently plans to write.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest moments. The specificity of the wrong analogy (goldfish + frozen pond = bullying survival guide) is both absurd and oddly coherent. The pivot to saving it for a children's book adds another layer of absurdity. The joke has a perfect three-part structure: setup, wrong analogy, unexpected salvage plan. Rachel's character voice is well-served here.

jokes.text: This is not a marriage! This is the world's worst hangover!
jokes.setup: Ross insists their situation is 'a difference of opinion within a marriage.'
jokes.punchline: Rachel reframes the entire marriage as simply a consequence of excessive drinking — 'the world's worst hangover.'
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. 'This is not a marriage! This is the world's worst hangover!' has the economy, specificity, and energy of a truly quotable line. It crystallizes the entire absurdity of the situation in nine words. The structure — denial + reframe — is clean, and the exaggeration ('world's worst') lands with appropriate comic force. This approaches but doesn't quite hit the 9+ tier — it's excellent episode-level writing, solidly at the 8 craft benchmark.

jokes.text: Hey, hey...is there any such thing as an annulment shower?
jokes.setup: Rachel has finally convinced Ross to get the annulment; the tension is resolved.
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately tries to find the upside — maybe there's an annulment gift-giving custom that could net him some presents, like a bridal shower.
jokes.explanation: Good callback to Ross's earlier materialist argument about keeping presents. Even in defeat, Ross is angling for the gift-giving angle. The phrase 'annulment shower' is a funny coinage, and it's very Ross to pivot immediately to the consolation prize.

jokes.text: I have your address and phone number. / I have your name and the fact that you're a drifter. / So ball's pretty much in your court.
jokes.setup: The hitchhiker is getting dropped off at a train station; they exchange contact information.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe takes stock of what each party has and concludes — 'ball's pretty much in your court' — with the satisfied tone of someone who clearly has negotiating leverage.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's power-move assessment of the information exchange is very funny. 'The fact that you're a drifter' as a catalogued piece of information she possesses — along with 'ball's pretty much in your court' — makes Phoebe sound like a negotiator who has the hitchhiker figured out. Great character economy.

jokes.text: Joey sings 'Space Oddity' (David Bowie) in an attempt to get Phoebe to forgive him.
jokes.setup: Joey is trying to make it up to Phoebe for sleeping through the road trip; he decides to sing to her.
jokes.punchline: Joey serenading Phoebe with a soaring, earnest rock vocal — which Phoebe admits she can't resist — is both funny and oddly sweet. The choice of song is incongruously dramatic for the context.
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in Joey's earnest use of a dramatic rock ballad as a peace offering, and Phoebe's immediate capitulation ('That's not fair. You know I can't resist that beautiful voice'). The scene works more through performance than writing.

jokes.text: Now I know that you think being awake is an important part of friendship.
jokes.setup: Joey is apologizing to Phoebe for sleeping through the entire road trip.
jokes.punchline: Joey frames consciousness as a novel friendship expectation — 'being awake is an important part of friendship' — as if this is a Phoebe-specific preference rather than a universal assumption.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. Joey's framing of wakefulness as a 'you think' — an idiosyncratic preference of Phoebe's rather than a basic social expectation — is perfectly absurd character comedy. The delivery would be earnest and apologetic, making it even funnier. High originality, excellent economy.

jokes.text: So I will strive to stay awake for as long as I know you. / You can still sleep at night and stuff.
jokes.setup: Joey promises to make it up to Phoebe by staying awake.
jokes.punchline: He makes a grand sweeping promise to stay awake 'for as long as he knows her' — an impossible commitment — and then immediately carves out 'at night and stuff,' revealing how quickly the promise deflates.
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-beat joke. The grandiose promise builds up beautifully, and 'You can still sleep at night and stuff' demolishes it perfectly. The structure — big commitment → immediate hedge → comfortable middle ground — is tight. Joey's earnest inability to maintain even a rhetorical promise is perfectly him.

jokes.text: I got a good one. I thought about it since Kansas. / Okay. / Is it...a kind of hot sandwich? / Yes. / Is it a meatball sub? / That is incredible! You are the master!
jokes.setup: Phoebe has been thinking of a 20 Questions answer since Kansas — building anticipation for a fiendishly difficult category.
jokes.punchline: Joey guesses it in one — 'a kind of hot sandwich?' → 'Is it a meatball sub?' — and they celebrate as if he's performed a miracle of intuition.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The setup — Phoebe has been mentally preparing her 20 Questions answer for hundreds of miles — creates the expectation of a brilliantly obscure category. The payoff is that Joey guesses it immediately and correctly with his very first question, 'a kind of hot sandwich?' Their shared ecstatic celebration of his 'mastery' is the cherry on top. Perfect character integration: Joey thinks in food, Phoebe chose food, neither finds this remarkable. The rewatch bonus comes from the callback to Phoebe's portentous 'use them wisely' earlier.

jokes.text: I got a good one. I thought about it since Kansas. / Okay. / Is it... a kind of hot sandwich? / Yes. / Is it a meatball sub? / That is incredible! You are the master!
jokes.setup: Phoebe has been thinking of a 20 Questions answer since Kansas; Joey takes his turn guessing
jokes.punchline: Joey guesses 'meatball sub' in two questions — which Phoebe calls incredible — but the joke is that his entire thought process was categorically food-based from question one, making a correct answer inevitable
jokes.explanation: The layered joke: (1) Joey's first guess is immediately 'a hot sandwich' — revealing his entire cognitive repertoire is food; (2) 'meatball sub' is the specific, correct answer; (3) Phoebe's genuinely impressed 'you are the master' treats his food-narrowing as genius. Perfect character integration for Joey — of course he'd solve any 20 Questions riddle as long as the answer is food.

jokes.text: Bug!
jokes.setup: Joey and Phoebe are driving and playing games, now in a cheerful groove.
jokes.punchline: Joey suddenly yells 'Bug!' — implying he's just driven through/caught a bug — an abrupt physical moment that breaks the idyllic mood.
jokes.explanation: One-word visual gag. The comedy is entirely in the abruptness and the implied physical moment. Maximum economy (one word) but limited craft — it's a sight gag that relies entirely on performance.

jokes.text: Enough already! / Well, you didn't have to catch them!
jokes.setup: Joey is catching bugs on the road trip; Phoebe is exasperated.
jokes.punchline: Joey's defense is that Phoebe didn't have to catch them — implying she did catch some bugs, and the criticism of his bug-catching is therefore hypocritical.
jokes.explanation: Quick escalation on the bug gag. The reveal that both of them were catching bugs — and that Joey's defense is that Phoebe had a choice — adds a layer to the visual comedy. 'You didn't have to catch them' is a funny line because it implies the entire activity was optional and they both indulged.

jokes.text: You look like you're.. / Don't say it! / Don't even think it. / All right. / Chandler, enjoy your handful.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica are back in their apartment; Chandler appears to be doing something (likely holding a handful of Monica's things or making a mess).
jokes.punchline: Monica cuts off Chandler's observation, forbids him from even thinking it, and then delivers 'Chandler, enjoy your handful' — a dismissal that implies he looks ridiculous and she's making him sit with the embarrassment.
jokes.explanation: The joke relies heavily on a visual we can't see from the transcript, but 'enjoy your handful' as a parting shot is a good line. The rewatch bonus applies because viewers who know the visual will get more from it. The 'don't even think it' escalation is a nice touch.

jokes.text: Should we just get married? / All the signs are telling us to do it. / I'm sick of the signs.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica have been using 'signs' to decide their relationship fate; Monica asks if they should just get married.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's 'I'm sick of the signs' — delivered as genuine exasperation — punctures the romantic mysticism they've been using to avoid making a real decision.
jokes.explanation: Chandler cutting through the romantic mysticism with weary pragmatism is in character. The scene has emotional weight underneath the humor, which makes the joke land more gently than some others.

jokes.text: I don't want change, do you? / No. / Then nothing changes! Everything stays the same! / Go unpack. It's been three days, and it drives me insane!
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica agree that nothing should change between them; Monica agrees enthusiastically.
jokes.punchline: Monica immediately demands Chandler unpack — 'it's been three days, and it drives me insane' — revealing that her idea of 'nothing changes' is very specific and includes her orderly home staying orderly.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Monica moment. The pivot from 'nothing changes!' to 'unpack immediately!' in the same breath reveals her character — her need for order overrides even her stated principles. The specificity of 'three days' makes it funnier. High character integration.

jokes.text: Jeez, relax, it's not like we're mar..
jokes.setup: Monica barks at Chandler to unpack; he starts to snap back with 'it's not like we're married—'
jokes.punchline: He catches himself mid-word as the irony hits — given their situation with Chandler moving in and their almost-marriage — and the unfinished sentence is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Excellent moment of dramatic irony. The unfinished sentence lands because the audience knows exactly what he was about to say and why he stopped. The cut-off 'mar—' is a perfect economy of comedy — maximum meaning with minimum words. The pause that follows (marked by [20:28]) is the comedic beat where the audience laughs. Strong structure.

jokes.text: What if we live together, and you get what I'm saying?
jokes.setup: Chandler is trying to propose that Monica and he move in together without saying it directly.
jokes.punchline: He trails off with 'and you get what I'm saying' — unable to actually say the words 'move in together,' instead hoping Monica will finish the thought.
jokes.explanation: Chandler's emotional avoidance — unable to say the commitment out loud even when suggesting it — is in perfect character. The trailing 'you get what I'm saying' as a substitute for the actual words is a good character beat.

jokes.text: Now go out and christen it! / Go out and come back in! / Door hasn't been locked in five years, but okay.
jokes.setup: Monica gives Chandler a key to her apartment and excitedly tells him to 'christen it' by going out and coming back in.
jokes.punchline: Chandler dryly notes that the door hasn't been locked in five years — the key is a romantic gesture for a lock that's been functionally useless.
jokes.explanation: Good joke grounded in Friends lore — the unlocked apartment door is a known running element of the show, and Chandler lampshading it here as meta-commentary is both funny and self-aware. 'Five years' is the specific detail that sells it.

jokes.text: The key broke in the lock, and I can't get in. / Wait. Oh, my God, I can't get out! / This isn't a sign! / No, it's a very old key! / It's an old key! / Oh, my God, it's old! / I love you.
jokes.setup: Chandler has gone out to 'christen' the key; it breaks in the lock.
jokes.punchline: The escalating key disaster — Chandler locked out, Monica locked in — culminates in both of them frantically defending the sign-neutrality of the broken key, and then Chandler ending with 'I love you' through the door.
jokes.explanation: Strong payoff on the key setup. The broken key could easily be read as a 'sign' against them living together — which both characters frantically deny in unison. The simultaneous 'it's a very old key!' defense is funny, and 'I love you' through a door they're both trapped by is a perfect emotional button. Good callback to Chandler's warning about the old lock.

jokes.text: Are you hugging the door right now? / No. / Yeah, yeah, me neither.
jokes.setup: After 'I love you' through the door, Chandler asks Monica if she's hugging the door.
jokes.punchline: Monica denies it; Chandler agrees he's also not hugging the door — both clearly lying, both hugging the door.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best closing jokes. The simultaneous denial — 'No. / Yeah, yeah, me neither' — is a perfect mutual lie that the audience knows is false. The image of both of them hugging a door from opposite sides is both funny and genuinely sweet. The deadpan delivery of 'Yeah, yeah, me neither' (Chandler's self-conscious retreat from sentimentality) is classic Chandler. High quotability, excellent economy.

jokes.text: So did everything go all right with the annulment? / Oh, yeah. No problems. It's all taken care of. / Ross, thank you.
jokes.setup: Rachel asks if Ross handled the annulment as promised
jokes.punchline: Ross lies to Rachel's face — 'No problems, all taken care of' — when the audience will shortly learn he did NOT get the annulment
jokes.explanation: Setup joke — it's not fully funny yet because the punchline comes later (joke 67). Functions primarily to make the reveal more impactful. Gets rewatch bonus because on rewatch you hear 'it's all taken care of' knowing it's a lie.

jokes.text: You wanna hear something weird? / Always. / I didn't get the annulment. / What? / We're still married. / Don't tell Rachel. See you later.
jokes.setup: Ross told Rachel he would get the annulment; now he casually confesses to Phoebe that he didn't.
jokes.punchline: The cheerful 'Don't tell Rachel. See you later.' is the punchline — Ross treating a massive deception with breezy casualness, as if he's left Phoebe in charge of a minor errand.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best and most memorable moments. The structure is perfect: casual check-in → confident reassurance → shocking reversal → 'Don't tell Rachel. See you later.' The final line's breezy non-sequitur energy is what makes it land so hard. Ross's self-serving obliviousness is at its peak here — he's perfectly aware of what he's doing and doesn't care in the slightest. The scene closes the episode on a great comedic shock. Phoebe's 'What?' is the audience's reaction mirrored on screen. Scores at or above the 8.0 craft anchor benchmark.

jokes.text: Nice job, Joe. You're quite the craftsman!
jokes.setup: Joey has attempted to fix the broken key in Monica's door; it still doesn't work.
jokes.punchline: Monica's dry 'Nice job, Joe. You're quite the craftsman!' — delivered over a completely failed repair — is sarcasm deployed with perfect economy.
jokes.explanation: Clean sarcastic button on the episode's final scene. Monica's dry delivery of genuine-sounding praise for a failure is a classic ironic compliment. Good economy; the word 'craftsman' is specifically funny given the context of a broken key.

tmdb_overview: Ross and Rachel experience the world’s worst hangover when they realize they’ve gotten married.  Chandler and Monica back away from their own altar plans.  Phoebe and Joey head back to New York in the taxi cab.
insight: Post-Vegas hangover episode coasts on character charm over comedic momentum.
